1. e4 {The king's pawn, two moves.} e5 {The same.} 2. c3 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.
(a) NOTE: This pawn is very ill played at the second move, because, by pushing your queen's pawn
two steps, you again secure the advantage of the move.} d5 {The queen's pawn, two moves.} 3.
exd5 {The pawn takes the pawn.} Qxd5 {The queen retakes the pawn.} 4. d3 {The queen's pawn, one
move. (b) NOTE: If, instead of this pawn, he had moved the king's knight to his king's second
square, you must have pushed your king's pawn forwards, and sustained it afterwards with your
king's bishop's pawn. p.18.} f5 {The king's bishop's pawn, two moves.} 5. f4 {The king's
bishop's pawn, two moves. (c) NOTE: If, instead of pushing this pawn, he had moved his queen's
bishop to his king's third square, you must have moved your king's bishop to his queen's third
square; and then the situation of the game would have been exactly as it is at the sixth move of
the second party: but, if he had attacked your queen with his queen's bishop's pawn, he would
have played very ill; because, the pawn, that is at the head of those which are on his queen's
side, would be left behind. Vide Note (1) on the 18th move of the third p.37. party:
nevertheless, we shall make it the subject of a back-game.} e4 {The king's pawn, one move. (d)
NOTE: It is a general rule, that you must avoid changing your king's pawn for your adversary's
king's bishop's pawn. You are to observe likewise the same rule with regard to your queen's pawn
against his queen's bishop's pawn; because it is demonstrated, that the king's and queen's pawns
are better than the others; since they, occupying the centre, hinder your adversary's pieces
from taking the most advantageous posts.} 6. d4 {The queen's pawn, one move. (e) NOTE: If,
instead of pushing this pawn, he had taken your king's pawn, you should, in that case have taken
his queen, and afterwards retaken his pawn; thus, hindering him from castling, you preserve the
attack upon him: but, as he could play his queen at his bishop's second square, we will make of
that move the subject of a back-game.} Qf7 {The queen, at her king's bishop's second square.} 7.
Be3 {The queen's bishop, at his king's third square.} Nf6 {The king's knight, at his bishop's
third square. Queen's} 8. Na3 {The queen's knight, at his king's second square.} Nd5 {The king's
knight, at his queen's fourth square.} 9. Bc4 {The king's bishop, at his queen's bishop's fourth
square.} c6 {The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} 10. Qb3 {The queen, at her knight's third
square.} Be6 {The queen's bishop, at his king's third square.} 11. Bxd5 {The king's bishop takes
the knight.} cxd5 {The pawn retakes the bishop. (f) NOTE: When you have two bodies of pawns
separated, you must always strengthen the strongest side, by uniting at the centre as many pawns
as possible.} 12. Ne2 {The king's knight, at his king's second square.} Bd6 {The king's bishop,
at his queen's third square.} 13. O-O {The king castles on his rook's side.} h6 {The king's
rook's pawn, one move.} 14. Qc2 {The queen, at her bishop's second square. (g) NOTE: His queen
being now of no use in that place, he removes her, to make room for his pawns, with a design to
push them upon you.} g5 {The king's knight's pawn, two moves.} 15. g3 {The king's knight's pawn,
one move.} g4 {The king's knight's pawn, one move. (h) NOTE: By the pushing of this pawn you
obstruct the game; but you will always have it in your power to make an opening with your king's
rook's pawn, as soon as your pieces are all ready to form and sustain your attack.} 16. b3 {The
queen's knight's pawn, one move.} Nc6 {The queen's knight, at his bishop's third square.} 17. c4
{The queen's bishop's pawn, one move.} O-O-O {The king castles on his queen's side. (i) NOTE:
You castle on your queen's side, to have a more free attack on your right wing: but, if instead
of castling you take the pawn offered to you, you thereby reunite in the centre your adversary's
pawns, which would prove very incommodious to your pieces.} 18. cxd5 {The pawn takes the pawn.}
Bxd5 {The bishop retakes the pawn.} 19. Nc4 {The queen's knight, at his queen's bishop's fourth
square.} h5 {The king's rook's pawn, one move.} 20. Nxd6+ {The knight takes the king's bishop.}
Rxd6 {The rook retakes the knight.} 21. Bf2 {The queen's bishop, at his king's bishop's second
square. (k) NOTE: Had you taken the knight with your queen's bishop, you had fallen into the
very error above mentioned, in reuniting his pawns in the centre.} h4 {The king's rook's pawn,
one move.} 22. b4 {The queen's knight's pawn, one move. (m) NOTE: He plays this pawn, to attack
the knight that covers your king, having nothing better in his power; for, by taking your pawn,
he would equally lose the game.} Rdh6 {The queen's rook, at its king's rook's third square.} 23.
b5 {The queen's knight's pawn, one move.} e3 {The king's pawn, one move.} 24. Be1 {The bishop,
at his king's square. (n) NOTE: If he takes the pawn with his bishop, he equally loses the
game.} hxg3 {The king's rook's pawn takes the pawn. 10).} 25. Bxg3 {The bishop retakes the
pawn.} Rxh2 {The rook takes the adverse king's rook's pawn.} 26. Bxh2 {The bishop takes the
rook.} Rxh2 {The king's rook takes the bishop.} 27. Kxh2 {The king takes the rook.} Qh7+ {The
queen gives check at the adverse king's rook's fourth square.} 28. Kg1 {The king, at his
knight's place, having no other.} Qh2+ {The queen gives check-mate.} *
